segments.speaker: John
segments.text: In our hypothetical course, Reinforcement Learning for Language-Model Agents, today's lecture is on “Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries.” Recent work such as “ZeroSearch: Incentivize the Search Capability of LLMs without Searching” and “SkillOS: Learning Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents” reflects a move toward training agents to search or organize reusable information. Researchers at Stanford, alongside a coauthor at Carnegie Mellon, ask what changes when a corpus is prepared before questions arrive. Yes, Noah?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Hi Professor, does this mean the system builds a search index before it knows what anyone will ask?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: That’s a useful starting point, but the workspace is more than an index. A builder agent turns raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthesized files, folders, summaries, and links back to sources. Later, a separate, frozen answering agent uses that workspace to answer questions. The builder does not see the future evaluation questions, so it must organize material for a range of possible needs rather than optimize for one known query.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Quick question: why not just use a fixed hierarchy or knowledge graph?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The authors argue that fixed structures can encode assumptions about what relationships matter. A hierarchy designed around one schema may make the wrong abstractions easy to find and others hard to represent. Instead, the builder learns which artifacts and groupings help downstream answering. It can create files, merge related files into higher-level summaries, delete unhelpful synthetic files, or stop. Raw documents remain available, so the system does not have to trust summaries as complete.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: So the main contribution is learning how to organize documents, not just writing better summaries?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Exactly. The paper treats corpus curation as a trainable behavior and judges it by whether another agent can answer questions more accurately. That separates the builder’s job from the answerer’s job. Provenance links connect synthetic files to their sources, and the answering agent is instructed to consult raw documents when summaries leave out needed details. The result is a reusable workspace with both synthesized navigation and a path back to evidence.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The builder’s state is the current filesystem, and its edits are actions in a finite-horizon reinforcement-learning problem. In the general formulation, the objective accounts for downstream answer accuracy along with costs such as construction effort, file reads, and answer-time tokens. In practice, the main training run sets explicit cost and navigation penalties to zero. That distinction matters: the reported results show improved answerability, but not that the builder learned to minimize construction cost.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Can you clarify how the system gets a learning signal if future questions are hidden from the builder?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The training process uses sampled probe queries to estimate whether the current workspace supports answering, but those queries are hidden from the builder itself. The system checks answerability every 8 builder turns, up to 4 times in a trajectory, and also provides a terminal reward for answer correctness. The policy is optimized with G-R-P-O. Dense feedback from edits helps training, while the paper explains that, without discounting, those edit rewards add up to the same overall objective as a final-workspace reward.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: How does it compare with retrieval systems on the main benchmark?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: On BrowseComp-Plus, the trained builder reaches reported accuracy of 0.75 with a quen three point five, four-billion answering model, and 0.77 with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite. Strong embedding and reranking baselines score 0.42 and 0.44 with the first model, and 0.30 and 0.42 with the second. The paper summarizes the overall gain over its strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines as 33 percentage points, though the exact difference varies by model and comparison.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Wait, if the workspace is bigger, does it actually save inference cost?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Not necessarily for each question. In a repeated-question evaluation, the trained workspace raises accuracy from 0.242 for the base builder to 0.637, but the answerer also reads more files and tokens: 26.9 files and 9,346 tokens per query, versus 2.72 files and 1,238 tokens. The authors estimate that, at 10 questions per corpus, the trained approach uses 33.8% fewer recorded tokens per expected correct answer. Their projected crossover is 31 questions, with a bootstrap interval from 18 to 54.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: So that advantage depends on reusing the same corpus enough times?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Yes. Construction is an upfront expense, and the benefit depends on how often a workspace is reused. The paper also tests transfer on the Bright benchmark, with workspaces built for AOPS, Biology, and Stack Overflow. The trained builder averages 52% pass at one and about 67% pass at three across those domains, with particularly strong results on Stack Overflow. These findings support transfer across the tested settings, not a guarantee for every domain or future question distribution.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Could the summaries still mislead the answering agent if they omit a crucial detail?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: That is a real limitation of any compressed representation. The system addresses it by preserving raw documents and linking synthetic files to their sources, so the answerer can inspect original evidence when a summary is insufficient. The workspace also grows substantially: on Bright, the trained builder creates an average of 53.4 active synthetic files, compared with 4.8 for the base builder. More structure can help navigation, but it also brings construction and maintenance questions that this evaluation does not settle.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The broader shift is from asking only how an agent searches a corpus at query time to asking how it can prepare a corpus for many future searches. That complements agentic retrieval, including hierarchical interfaces such as A-RAG, while differing from skill-curation work such as SkillOS: here, the reusable resource is an organized external document collection. The paper’s evidence suggests learned curation can help a frozen answerer, but its cost trade-offs and changing-corpus behavior remain open research problems.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Would the next step be to update workspaces as documents and question patterns change?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: That is one important direction, along with testing much larger collections and deciding when to bypass synthetic material and search raw sources directly. The study focuses on static corpora and benchmarks, while real deployments face updates, uneven reuse, and questions no summary anticipated. The central takeaway is that document organization can itself be learned and evaluated through downstream usefulness. A workspace is not a substitute for evidence; it is a reusable map that must remain connected to it. Thanks for listening. If you have any further questions, ask our AI assistant or drop a comment.
